stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 8.1 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 304 K and 0.95 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 34.0 mL of 0.15 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.2 M NaOH.
7.4 g of $$\ce{CaCl2}$$ dissolves in 72 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 3.4 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Fe electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Fe^{2+}}$$ and a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Fe^{2+} + 2e- -> Fe}$$ E° = -0.44 V; $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V.
The photoelectron spectra of C (Z = 6) and N (Z = 7) are compared.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 27 g. The actual yield is 19.2 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the pH of a 0.05 M solution of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 1 × 0.05 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 15.2 g. The actual yield is 9.9 g. What is the percent yield?
For the elementary step 2NO + Cl₂ → 2NOCl, what is the rate law?

options.why: Correct. Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

options.text: It cannot be determined without experiment

questions.explanation: Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 91 g of $$\ce{KCl}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 74.55 g/mol.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{CaO}$$ or $$\ce{NaCl}$$?

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{NaCl}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{NaCl}$$, because its ions have larger charges

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaCl has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
Which is the ground-state electron configuration of titanium (Ti, Z = 22)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 22 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.792 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A weak acid HA has pKa = 8.7. In a solution at pH 6.1, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.9 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.1 mol Ar at a total pressure of 2.4 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.04 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 275 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A solution has an absorbance of 0.234 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 234 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size
Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 565 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: How can an unfavorable reaction (ΔG positive) be made to occur?

options.text: By coupling it to a favorable reaction so the total ΔG is negative

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 17. What is K for the reaction multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of chlorine shows two peaks: mass 35 with relative abundance 35% and mass 37 with 65%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0165 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 36 kJ/mol, the transition state at 97 kJ/mol and the products at 175 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 61, ΔH = 139, reverse Ea = -78 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of C in $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 0.6. A mixture has [A] = 0.9 M, [B] = 0.4 M and [C] = 0.1 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.0278
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.0278, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.0278
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.278
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K

questions.stem: Which indicator is best for titrating acetic acid with NaOH (equivalence pH ≈ 8.7)?

options.why: Correct. Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.explanation: Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: He 4, Cl2 70.9, CH4 16, N2 28.

questions.stem: A 29.8 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 36.4 mL of 0.225 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 497 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: Why is the radius of F⁻ larger than that of F?

options.text: The added electron increases electron–electron repulsion with the same nuclear charge
options.why: Correct. Anions are larger than their atoms.

options.text: F⁻ has an additional electron shell

questions.explanation: Anions are larger than their atoms.

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.
Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.169 mol of solute in enough water to make 860 mL of solution?
For $$\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$$, $$\ce{N2O5}$$ is consumed at 0.26 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NO2}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 4/2.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{BF3}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 5.6. In a solution at pH 8.6, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.3 mol N₂, 0.7 mol O₂ and 0.4 mol Ar at a total pressure of 2.2 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.why: Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 8.6. In a solution at pH 5.6, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{PCl3}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.

options.text: Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel

options.why: Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Nonpolar, because it has no polar bonds
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

questions.explanation: PCl3 is trigonal pyramidal; the dipoles do not cancel.

questions.stem: 147 g of water at 78 °C is mixed with 27 g of water at 15 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (0.96).

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.014 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 80 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 12.6 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 4210 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.2 mol N₂, 0.5 mol O₂ and 0.4 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.9 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: What volume does 1.93 mol of gas occupy at 25 atm and 316 K?

options.why: 22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.
Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.5 M solution of formic acid (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 18. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 112 kJ/mol, the transition state at 176 kJ/mol and the products at 145 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 64, ΔH = 33, reverse Ea = 31 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.2) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 43.8 mL. What is the pH after 21.9 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 466, 2796, 4865, 7589 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 1 electron, so it has 1 valence electron.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -125 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -348 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Pb/$$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$ and Ag/$$\ce{Ag+}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.text: Ag, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.

questions.explanation: Pb (E° -0.13 V) is oxidized at the anode; Ag is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔH° = 185 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 123 J/(mol·K). Above what temperature is it thermodynamically favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ).
Correct. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (with ΔH in J).

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.45 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 6.35) and 0.18 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.04 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -17 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 6.86; K = 955. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 0.9 M and [I₂] = 0.8 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.04 M. What is K?
A reaction has ΔG° = −50 kJ/mol but does not occur noticeably at room temperature. The best explanation is:

options.why: Negative ΔG° means K greater than 1.

options.text: It has a high activation energy, so it is under kinetic control
options.why: Correct. Favorable is not the same as fast.

questions.explanation: Favorable is not the same as fast.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 6 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6 : 2. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}\,4s^{2}$$, which has 20 electrons.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{PbI2}$$ is 7.1 \times 10^{-9}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
What is the rate law?

options.why: Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$$, 77 g of $$\ce{Fe}$$ reacts with 53 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. Fe is the limiting reactant.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$$.

options.why: Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Exothermic: the solution warmed, so energy was released.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Fe²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.01 M F⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with F⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of N.
Explain why the 1s peak of N has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of C.

rubric.criterion: N has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: N has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: C: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
